title: Alertmanager & Custom Alerting Rules
summary: Prometheus collects metrics, but it doesn't send notifications — that's Alertmanager's job. PrometheusRule CRDs let you define alert conditions as PromQL expressions; Alertmanager routes firing alerts to the right receiver (Slack, PagerDuty, email) based on labels. This lesson covers writing alert rules, tuning severity and for duration, configuring routing trees, inhibition, silences, and building runbooks.

sections.title: Alerting architecture: Prometheus → Alertmanager → Receivers
sections.body:
## What is alerting and why is the Prometheus/Alertmanager split important?

Prometheus collects metrics by scraping targets at a regular interval (typically every 15 seconds). It also evaluates **alert rules** — PromQL expressions that describe an undesirable condition, such as a high error rate or a node running out of disk space. When an expression evaluates to true for a sustained period, Prometheus considers the alert FIRING and sends a notification to **Alertmanager**.

The reason Prometheus and Alertmanager are separate processes — not a single monolith — is architectural. Prometheus is a single-purpose metrics engine; doing alert delivery well requires a completely different set of concerns: deduplication (two Prometheus instances in an HA pair may both fire the same alert), grouping (batching 50 pod restart alerts into one Slack message rather than flooding the channel), routing (critical database alerts should page the DBA team, not the frontend team), silencing (suppress alerts during a planned maintenance window), and inhibition (suppress symptom alerts when the root-cause alert is already firing). Alertmanager handles all of these.

In the kube-prometheus-stack, alert rules are defined as **PrometheusRule** CRDs — Kubernetes objects that the Prometheus Operator watches and automatically loads into Prometheus's configuration. This means alert rules are version-controlled YAML in your repository, reviewed in pull requests, and applied via the same `kubectl apply` workflow as your application deployments. There is no separate web UI where someone can quietly add or modify alert rules without a trace.

Before running the commands in this section, understand the three alert states: INACTIVE (the condition is not met), PENDING (the condition is met but the `for` duration has not elapsed yet), and FIRING (the condition has been continuously true for the full `for` duration and Alertmanager has been notified). The PENDING→FIRING transition is the key noise-reduction mechanism — it filters out transient spikes.

**The alerting pipeline:**

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                             │
│  PrometheusRule (CRD)                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │  expr: rate(http_requests_total{code="5xx"}[5m])  │       │
│  │         > 0.05                                    │       │
│  │  for: 2m                                          │       │
│  │  labels: { severity: warning }                    │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
│           │ evaluates every 15s                             │
│           ▼                                                 │
│  Prometheus (evaluates rules, sends to Alertmanager)        │
│           │ fires when expr is true for 'for' duration      │
│           ▼                                                 │
│  Alertmanager (dedup, group, route, silence, inhibit)       │
│           │                                                 │
│     ┌─────┼─────┐                                           │
│     ▼     ▼     ▼                                           │
│   Slack PD  Email  (receivers)                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Alert states:**

```
INACTIVE  → PromQL expression is false (no alert)
PENDING   → Expression became true, but 'for' duration not elapsed yet
FIRING    → Expression was true for the entire 'for' duration → sent to Alertmanager
```

**Why the `for` duration matters:**

```yaml
# Without 'for': alert fires on the first evaluation where expr is true
# Causes alert flapping on transient spikes
expr: rate(http_errors[1m]) > 0

# With 'for: 2m': must be continuously true for 2 minutes
# Filters out brief spikes, reduces noise
expr: rate(http_errors[1m]) > 0
for: 2m
```

**Alertmanager's responsibilities:**

```
Deduplication   — multiple Prometheus instances may fire the same alert; Alertmanager dedupes
Grouping        — batch related alerts into one notification (all pods in same service)
Routing         — send critical alerts to PagerDuty, warnings to Slack
Silencing       — suppress alerts during maintenance windows
Inhibition      — suppress child alerts when a parent alert fires
                  (e.g., suppress per-pod alerts when the whole cluster is down)
```

sections.title: Writing PrometheusRule resources
sections.body:
## How do you write alert rules that are useful rather than noisy?

Writing a PromQL expression that fires when a metric exceeds a threshold is the easy part. Writing alert rules that pages the right person with actionable information, at the right time, with low false-positive rates — that is the skill that separates mature observability practices from alert-fatigued teams.

A well-written alert rule has four properties. It is **actionable**: the person who receives the alert knows exactly what to do, because the annotation links to a runbook that explains it. It is **accurate**: it fires on real user impact, not on metrics that are correlated with problems but not causal (CPU usage is a common trap — a busy CPU is not necessarily a problem if response times are fine). It is **timely**: the `for` duration is calibrated so that transient spikes don't trigger the alert, but real sustained problems are caught before they escalate. And it is **proportionate**: the severity label reflects how urgently a human needs to respond — critical means page someone now, warning means investigate within an hour.

The **Watchdog** alert — an expression that is always true (`vector(1)`) — deserves special mention. It exists to test the alerting pipeline itself. If Prometheus stops scraping, or Alertmanager goes down, or the Slack webhook stops working, your real alerts will silently fail to deliver. The Watchdog alert fires continuously, and you configure a service (like PagerDuty's Dead Man's Snitch, or a similar heartbeat receiver) to expect it. If it stops arriving, the monitoring system itself is broken. This is a critical operational pattern that many teams neglect until they discover — during an incident — that their alerts were not actually being delivered.

The template functions available in alert annotations (`humanize`, `humanizePercentage`, `humanizeDuration`) transform raw numeric values into human-readable strings. An annotation that says "error rate is 0.12345" is less useful under pressure than one that says "error rate is 12.35%".

**PrometheusRule is a CRD — define alert rules as Kubernetes objects:**

```yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: application-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
  labels:
    # Must match the Prometheus operator's ruleSelector
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  groups:
  - name: application.rules
    interval: 30s     # How often to evaluate this group (default: global interval)
    rules:

    # ── Error rate alert ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - alert: HighErrorRate
      expr: |
        sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) by (service)
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (service)
        > 0.05
      for: 2m
      labels:
        severity: warning
        team: backend
      annotations:
        summary: "High error rate on {{ $labels.service }}"
        description: "{{ $labels.service }} has {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} error rate (threshold: 5%)"
        runbook_url: "https://runbooks.company.com/high-error-rate"

    # ── Latency alert ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - alert: SlowRequests
      expr: |
        histogram_quantile(0.99,
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)
        ) > 2
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: "P99 latency > 2s on {{ $labels.service }}"
        description: "P99 request latency is {{ $value | humanizeDuration }} on {{ $labels.service }}"

    # ── Pod crash alert ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - alert: PodCrashLooping
      expr: |
        rate(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[15m]) * 60 * 15 > 3
      for: 1m
      labels:
        severity: critical
      annotations:
        summary: "Pod {{ $labels.namespace }}/{{ $labels.pod }} is crash-looping"
        description: "Container {{ $labels.container }} has restarted {{ $value | humanize }} times in 15m"

    # ── Capacity alerts ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    - alert: PodMemoryHigh
      expr: |
        container_memory_working_set_bytes{container!=""}
        / container_spec_memory_limit_bytes{container!=""} > 0.85
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: "Container {{ $labels.container }} memory at {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}"

    # ── Dead man's switch (ensure alerting pipeline is working) ──────────
    - alert: Watchdog
      expr: vector(1)
      labels:
        severity: none
      annotations:
        summary: "Alerting pipeline is functioning"
        description: "This alert always fires — if you stop receiving it, the pipeline is broken"
```

**Template functions available in annotations:**

```
{{ $value }}                    → raw numeric value
{{ $value | humanize }}         → human-readable (1.23k, 4.56M)
{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} → 12.34%
{{ $value | humanizeDuration }} → 2m 30s
{{ $labels.pod }}               → label value
{{ $externalLabels.cluster }}   → Prometheus external labels
```

sections.title: Routing trees and inhibition
sections.body:
## How does Alertmanager decide where to send each alert?

Alertmanager's routing configuration is a tree of matchers. Every incoming alert starts at the root of the tree and walks down, matching rules until it finds a node with no further matching children — that node's receiver handles the alert. This tree structure allows you to express sophisticated routing logic: send all alerts to a default Slack channel by default, but route critical alerts to PagerDuty, route database-specific alerts to the DBA Slack channel, and silently drop informational alerts that have no receiver.

The grouping and timing parameters on each routing node are as important as the receiver assignment. `group_by` determines which label values must match for alerts to be batched together — grouping by `[alertname, namespace]` means all `PodCrashLooping` alerts in the `production` namespace are delivered as a single message, rather than one message per pod. `group_wait` is a deliberate delay before sending the first notification for a new group, to allow related alerts to accumulate and be included. `repeat_interval` controls how often a still-firing alert resends its notification — 12 hours for a warning is reasonable, but 4 hours for a critical alert may be more appropriate.

**Inhibition** is the mechanism that prevents alert storms from overwhelming on-call engineers. In a distributed system, when a node goes down, every pod on that node starts crash-looping, every service those pods provide starts returning errors, and every consumer of those services starts logging timeouts. Without inhibition, a single node failure generates dozens of alerts — all of which are symptoms of the same root cause. Inhibition rules suppress the symptom alerts when the root-cause alert is already firing, so on-call sees one alert (NodeDown) rather than fifty (PodCrashLooping × 50). Designing good inhibition rules requires understanding your system's failure modes and the relationships between them.

**Alertmanager configuration — the routing tree:**

```yaml
# alertmanager.yaml (mounted as a Secret in kube-prometheus-stack)
global:
  resolve_timeout: 5m
  slack_api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/services/...'

route:
  # Default receiver — catches everything not matched below
  receiver: slack-warnings
  group_by: [alertname, namespace]  # Group alerts with same labels into one message
  group_wait: 30s      # Wait this long for more alerts before sending first notification
  group_interval: 5m   # How long to wait before sending update on a group
  repeat_interval: 12h # How long before re-notifying a still-firing alert

  routes:
  # Critical alerts → PagerDuty (immediate)
  - match:
      severity: critical
    receiver: pagerduty
    group_wait: 0s       # Send immediately — no waiting
    repeat_interval: 4h

  # Database alerts → dedicated DBA channel
  - match_re:
      alertname: "(Postgres|Redis|MySQL).*"
    receiver: slack-database

  # Suppress Watchdog alert (it's informational only)
  - match:
      alertname: Watchdog
    receiver: blackhole

receivers:
- name: slack-warnings
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#alerts-warning'
    title: '{{ template "slack.title" . }}'
    text: '{{ template "slack.text" . }}'
    send_resolved: true

- name: pagerduty
  pagerduty_configs:
  - routing_key: '{{ secrets.pagerduty_key }}'
    severity: '{{ .CommonLabels.severity }}'
    description: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}'

- name: slack-database
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#alerts-database'
    send_resolved: true

- name: blackhole  # Swallows alerts silently
```

**Inhibition rules — suppress child alerts during outages:**

```yaml
inhibit_rules:
# If the whole cluster is down (ClusterDown alert fires),
# suppress per-node and per-pod alerts (they're all symptoms, not causes)
- source_match:
    alertname: ClusterDown
    severity: critical
  target_match_re:
    alertname: "(NodeDown|PodCrashLooping|HighErrorRate).*"
  equal: [cluster]  # Only inhibit alerts with the same cluster label

# If a node is down, suppress pod alerts from that node
- source_match:
    alertname: NodeDown
    severity: critical
  target_match:
    alertname: PodCrashLooping
  equal: [node]
```

**Silences — suppress specific alerts for a time window:**

```bash
# Create a silence via Alertmanager API (for maintenance windows)
curl -s -X POST \
  http://alertmanager:9093/api/v2/silences \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "matchers": [
      {"name": "namespace", "value": "staging", "isRegex": false}
    ],
    "startsAt": "2026-05-13T02:00:00Z",
    "endsAt":   "2026-05-13T04:00:00Z",
    "createdBy": "ops-bot",
    "comment":   "Scheduled maintenance window"
  }'

# Or use the Alertmanager UI: http://alertmanager:9093
```

sections.title: Runbooks and alert quality
sections.body:
## What is a runbook and why is alert quality a DevOps concern?

A runbook is the operational documentation linked from an alert annotation that tells an on-call engineer what to do when that specific alert fires. Without a runbook, an alert at 3 AM means waking up, staring at a Grafana dashboard, and trying to remember what this metric means and what the remediation procedure is. With a well-written runbook, the same alert means following a checklist that was written during calm daylight hours by the engineer who designed the system.

Runbook quality directly affects how on-call engineers treat alerts. When runbooks are helpful and accurate, engineers trust the alerts and respond promptly. When runbooks are missing, outdated, or wrong, engineers start dismissing alerts without investigating — the definition of **alert fatigue**. Alert fatigue is a serious reliability risk: when on-call engineers stop trusting the alerting system, real incidents get missed or responded to slowly.

The broader concept of **alert quality** encompasses the full lifecycle of an alert: is it detecting a real user-impacting condition (not a metric that correlates with problems but isn't causal)? Is the threshold set appropriately (not so sensitive that it fires on normal variance, not so insensitive that problems escape detection)? Is the `for` duration tuned to filter transient spikes without delaying detection of sustained problems? Is the severity label accurate (not everything is critical)?

**SLO-based alerting** — alerting on error budget burn rate rather than raw error rate — represents the current best practice for high-scale production alerting. Instead of asking "is error rate above 1%?", it asks "are we consuming our error budget so fast that we will exhaust it within an hour?" This approach naturally handles traffic variability (a fixed 1% threshold is too sensitive at low traffic), focuses engineering attention on SLO-threatening conditions, and integrates directly with the practice of defining and tracking Service Level Objectives. The burn rate formula in this section implements exactly the multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting approach described in the Google SRE Workbook.

**A runbook is the documentation that answers: what do I do when this alert fires?**

Every alert should link to a runbook in its annotations. A good runbook:

```markdown
# HighErrorRate Runbook

## What fired
HTTP 5xx error rate exceeded 5% for 2 minutes on `{{ service }}`.

## Severity
Warning → investigate within 30 minutes
Critical → page on-call immediately

## Immediate checks
1. Check pod logs:
   kubectl logs -l app={{ service }} -n production --tail=50

2. Check recent deployments:
   kubectl rollout history deployment/{{ service }} -n production

3. Check downstream dependencies:
   kubectl get pods -n production   # Are all pods healthy?
   kubectl get events -n production # Any OOMKills or evictions?

## Likely causes
- Recent deployment introduced a regression → rollback:
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/{{ service }} -n production
- Database connection pool exhausted → check connection count
- Dependency (Redis, external API) is down → check dependency status
- Traffic spike exhausting replicas → check HPA and scale up

## Escalation
If not resolved in 30 minutes, escalate to {{ team }} via PagerDuty.
```

**Alert quality — signal vs noise:**

```
Good alert:
  ✓ Actionable: you know exactly what to do when it fires
  ✓ Urgent: represents a real user-impacting problem
  ✓ Accurate: rarely fires spuriously (no flapping)
  ✓ Has a runbook link

Bad alert:
  ✗ CPU > 50% — CPU usage alone doesn't mean users are impacted
  ✗'error' in logs — too noisy; logs always have errors
  ✗ No 'for' duration — fires on every transient spike
  ✗ No runbook — on-call doesn't know what to do

Alert fatigue:
  If on-call ignores alerts because they're always noisy,
  the entire alerting system becomes useless.
  Aim for: every fired alert requires a human action.
```

**SLO-based alerting (burn rate alerts):**

```yaml
# Alert on SLO burn rate rather than raw error rate
# If 5% error rate budget is consumed at 14x the normal rate,
# you'll exhaust it in 1 hour
- alert: ErrorBudgetBurnHigh
  expr: |
    (
      sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1h]))
      /
      sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h]))
    ) > (14 * 0.001)   # 14x burn rate, 0.1% error budget
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "Error budget burning fast — SLO at risk within 1 hour"
```

sections.title: Exercise: create and trigger an alert
sections.body:
## What you will practise

Reading about the PENDING → FIRING state transition is very different from watching it happen. This exercise gives you that experience: you write a PrometheusRule, watch it appear in the Prometheus rules UI, deploy a deliberately crash-looping pod, and observe the restart counter increment in real time until it crosses the threshold and the alert transitions through PENDING into FIRING in Alertmanager.

Two things to understand before you start. First, the `release: kube-prometheus-stack` label on the PrometheusRule metadata is not optional — it is how the Prometheus Operator's `ruleSelector` identifies which PrometheusRule objects to load into Prometheus's configuration. If this label is wrong or missing, your rule will be accepted by Kubernetes but silently ignored by Prometheus. Always verify that your rule appears in the Prometheus UI at `/rules` after applying it. Second, the `increase()` function in the alert expression measures the total increase in the restart counter over the 5-minute window — not the current value. A pod that has restarted 3 times in the last 5 minutes will have `increase(...[5m]) = 3`, regardless of its total lifetime restart count. This is the right function for detecting recent crash-loop behaviour without triggering on pods that had a restart months ago.

Create a PrometheusRule that fires when a pod has restarted more than once in 5 minutes, then trigger it.

```bash
# ── 1. Check current alerts ───────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get prometheusrules -n monitoring
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/alertmanager-operated 9093 &
# Open http://localhost:9093 to see Alertmanager UI

# ── 2. View existing PrometheusRule ──────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get prometheusrule kube-prometheus-stack-kubernetes-apps \
  -n monitoring -o yaml | grep -A10 'PodCrashLooping'

# ── 3. Create a custom alert rule ────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: learning-alerts
  namespace: monitoring
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  groups:
  - name: learning.rules
    rules:
    - alert: LearningPodRestarting
      expr: |
        increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{
          namespace="learning"
        }[5m]) > 1
      for: 30s
      labels:
        severity: warning
        namespace: learning
      annotations:
        summary: "Pod {{ $labels.pod }} restarting in learning namespace"
        description: "Container {{ $labels.container }} has restarted {{ $value }} times in 5m"
EOF

# ── 4. Verify Prometheus picked up the rule ───────────────────────────────
# Port-forward Prometheus
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/prometheus-operated 9090 &
# Open http://localhost:9090/rules and look for 'LearningPodRestarting'

# ── 5. Trigger the alert ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Deploy a crash-looping pod
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: crash-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo 'starting'; sleep 5; exit 1"]
  restartPolicy: Always
EOF

# ── 6. Watch restarts accumulate ──────────────────────────────────────────
watch kubectl get pod crash-pod -n learning
# RESTARTS column should increment every ~5 seconds

# ── 7. Check Prometheus for the firing alert ─────────────────────────────
# In http://localhost:9090/alerts look for LearningPodRestarting in PENDING/FIRING

# Query to confirm (in Prometheus UI):
# increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="learning",pod="crash-pod"}[5m])

# ── 8. Check Alertmanager ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
# After ~30 seconds it should appear in http://localhost:9093

# ── 9. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete pod crash-pod -n learning
kubectl delete prometheusrule learning-alerts -n monitoring
```

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `for: 2m` field in a PrometheusRule alert?
options: Repeat the alert notification every 2 minutes
The alert only fires if the expression has been continuously true for 2 minutes, reducing false positives from transient spikes
Pause alert evaluation for 2 minutes after the alert resolves
Group alerts that fire within 2 minutes of each other
questions.explanation: The `for` duration sets a minimum time the expression must be true before the alert transitions from PENDING to FIRING. Without it, a single-second CPU spike would fire an alert. With `for: 2m`, the condition must be sustained — dramatically reducing alert noise from transient issues.

questions.q: What does an inhibition rule in Alertmanager do?
options: Prevents an alert from firing more than once per hour
Suppresses alerts from being sent to receivers entirely
Suppresses child/symptom alerts when a parent/cause alert is firing
questions.explanation: Inhibition prevents alert storms. When a high-level alert fires (e.g., NodeDown), dozens of downstream alerts (pod restarts, high error rates) also fire — all as symptoms of the same cause. Inhibition suppresses those symptoms so on-call only sees the root cause alert.

questions.q: What is a 'dead man's switch' alert (like the Watchdog alert)?
options: An alert that fires when a critical service has been down for too long
An alert that always fires to verify the alerting pipeline itself is working
An alert with no receiver — used for testing
An alert that automatically pages on-call if not acknowledged
questions.explanation: A dead man's switch alert (Watchdog) is an alert expression that is always true (`vector(1)`). If you stop receiving this alert, it means the alerting pipeline itself is broken — Prometheus stopped scraping, Alertmanager is down, or the notification channel failed. You can use a service like PagerDuty's Dead Man's Snitch to expect this alert and page if it stops arriving.

sections.title: Challenge: build a complete alerting setup
sections.goal: Create a PrometheusRule with three alerts of different severities, configure a Slack receiver in Alertmanager (or a webhook receiver for testing), and write a runbook for your most critical alert.
hints: Use `webhook_configs` receiver in Alertmanager pointing to a local service for testing without real Slack — or use https://webhook.site to get a temporary URL
Patch the Alertmanager config Secret: `kubectl get secret alertmanager-kube-prometheus-stack-alertmanager -n monitoring -o yaml`
For the PrometheusRule label selector, check what labels Prometheus expects: `kubectl get prometheus -n monitoring -o yaml | grep ruleSelector`
Test your PromQL expressions in the Prometheus UI (/graph) before putting them in a rule
success_criteria: PrometheusRule resource exists in monitoring namespace with at least 3 alerts
Alerts have different severity labels (info, warning, critical)
Each alert has a summary and description annotation
Alertmanager routing tree has at least two routes based on severity
A runbook markdown file exists for the critical alert with immediate steps and likely causes
